title: Guest post: How extreme heat is ‘creeping’ from summer into autumn and spring - Carbon Brief
gist: A new study (Ivanovich et al. 2026, AGU Advances) finds that in more than half of the world's land area, extreme heat events are spreading from tightly-defined 1980s 'heat seasons' into two-month 'shoulder seasons' before and after them — asymmetrically by region and only partly explained by average warming — raising compound-hazard risks such as heat overlapping with US wildfire and Atlantic hurricane seasons.

themes.theme: Extreme heat is spreading beyond its traditional season

insights.claim: A study published in AGU Advances (Ivanovich et al., 2026) is the first to measure globally whether the calendar-year timing of extreme heat is changing, finding that in more than half of the world's land area, extreme heat events are spreading into 'shoulder seasons' outside the traditional heat season, though unevenly by location.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Establishes a quantified, peer-reviewed baseline that extreme-heat risk windows are widening beyond conventional summer planning periods — relevant for anyone pricing seasonal heat risk (insurance, utilities, agriculture, public health).
insights.quote: Extreme heat events are spreading out significantly in the calendar year in more than half of global land areas.

insights.claim: In the 1980s baseline period, extreme heat was tightly confined to a single season worldwide: about 93% of the world's land area saw more than 80% of its extreme dry-heat days occur within its traditional dry-heat season, a pattern that held even in the tropics where seasonal temperature swings are smaller.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete historical baseline against which the current shoulder-season creep can be measured and monitored going forward.
insights.quote: some 93% of the world’s land area experienced more than 80% of extreme dry-heat days during its traditional dry-heat season.

insights.claim: The creep of extreme heat into shoulder seasons is directionally uneven by region: western Europe, southern Africa and north-western India are seeing a larger share of extreme heat shift into the pre-season (spring-like) shoulder, while much of the US, eastern China, northern Africa and eastern Europe are seeing more shift into the post-season (autumn-like) shoulder.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Region-specific asymmetry means heat-risk preparedness (early warning systems, cooling infrastructure) must be tailored by geography and by season rather than applying a single global 'longer summer' assumption.

insights.claim: The study defines a location's 'local heat season' as the three consecutive months with the most extreme-heat events in the 1980s baseline, and 'shoulder seasons' as the two-month windows immediately before and after it, then tracks how the share of annual extreme-heat days falling in each window changed between the 1980s and 2015-2024 using MERRA2 reanalysis data, cross-checked against ERA5 reanalysis data for robustness.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A reusable, geography-agnostic methodology (local heat season plus shoulder-season tracking, cross-validated across two reanalysis datasets) that other researchers or risk modelers could apply to specific assets, crops, or regions of interest.

insights.claim: Extreme dry-heat and extreme humid-heat seasons at the same location are often offset from each other by about one month, a pattern especially pronounced in monsoon-influenced regions such as north-western Mexico and central India, where the extreme dry-heat season precedes the extreme humid-heat season.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Dry heat (more damaging to crops/ecosystems) and humid heat (more strenuous for humans) can require separately timed mitigation windows in monsoon regions rather than a single combined heat-season response.

themes.theme: What is driving the shoulder-season creep

insights.claim: A simple 'shift up' test — raising the 1980s baseline heat timeseries by the average local warming observed between 1980-89 and 2015-24 — explains the extension of extreme heat within the traditional heat season, but average annual warming alone cannot explain why the shoulder-season creep is asymmetric (favoring spring in some regions, autumn in others).
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Means simple global- or local-average warming trend models will misestimate where and when shoulder-season heat risk actually materializes — risk models for agriculture, insurance and utilities need region-specific drivers, not just an average-warming adjustment.
insights.quote: annual average warming alone cannot explain the uneven changes in how extreme heat is occurring in the shoulder seasons.

insights.claim: Candidate explanations for the asymmetric shoulder-season creep that the study flags as needing further regionally-focused research include long-term shifts in seasonal precipitation and soil moisture, land-use changes such as agricultural intensification or increased irrigation, and natural climate oscillations like the Pacific Decadal Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Names specific, trackable regional variables (soil moisture trends, irrigation expansion, PDO/AMO phase) that could serve as leading indicators for where shoulder-season heat risk will intensify next.
insights.locator: Long-term changes in seasonal precipitation and soil moisture

themes.theme: Compounding hazard risk and adaptation implications

insights.claim: Heat extremes that occur outside peak summer are often more dangerous because bodies are not yet acclimatized to heat and adaptive infrastructure such as air conditioning or public cooling centres may not yet be deployed, while heatwaves late in the year hit populations and infrastructure already strained by a long hot summer.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Implies mortality and health-system risk from shoulder-season heat is likely underestimated by preparedness systems built around a fixed summer window — actionable for public-health and disaster-response planning budgets.
insights.locator: Heat extremes that happen outside of the peak summer months

insights.claim: In the western US, the extension of the heat season further into autumn could increase its overlap with the wildfire season, while in the eastern US, a similar autumn extension of the heat season could increase overlap with the Atlantic hurricane season.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Specific, geography-tagged compound-hazard pathways (heat-wildfire in the west, heat-hurricane in the east) are directly relevant to catastrophe modeling and reinsurance pricing for US regional exposure.
insights.quote: extreme heat which stretches later into the year could increase the overlap between the extreme heat and wildfire seasons

insights.claim: Because multiple hazards occurring together or in quick succession are far more dangerous than isolated events, understanding how shifting seasonal hazard overlap is changing is described as essential for designing targeted climate adaptation strategies, including extending heat early-warning systems and cooling centres beyond the traditional summer months.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals likely future policy and infrastructure spending shifts toward extending heat early-warning systems and cooling-centre operations into spring and autumn, not just summer.
insights.quote: multiple hazards happening at once or in quick succession are much more dangerous than when they happen in isolation
